newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germans discontented with confusing reforms - poll.
newsitem.headline: Germans discontented with confusing reforms - poll.

text.p: German voters are increasingly discontented about political confusion in Bonn and split over whether Chancellor Helmut Kohl should force through tough economic reforms, a leading pollster said on Wednesday.

Renate Koecher of the Allensbach polling group said voters were confused and disoriented by a wave of reform proposals and counterproposals -- all part of Bonn's efforts to cut spending to qualify for Europe's planned monetary union (EMU).
Voters found the issues loaded down with power struggles over special interests, and were increasingly cynical about the debates and demonstrations they saw on the nightly news.
In the latest such example, coal miners on Wednesday ended three days of protests in Bonn after Kohl proposed slashing subsidies for the overpriced German coal industry.

Writing in the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung, Koecher said: "This outpouring of statements, criticism and counterproposals has led people to discuss reforms intensively... (but) with little knowledge and many pessimistic assumptions."
Koecher said most voters agreed that Germany's tax and pension systems needed to be overhauled -- but there were no proposals convincing enough to enjoy majority support.

"Whether one considers tax or pension reform, the health system reform or other social corrections -- there is little understanding for the goals, most people have negative opinions and there is little hope of seeing a satisfactory solution.
"There is a widespread feeling that people's own interests and their sense of justice are being ignored," she wrote.

Only 43 percent of voters believed Bonn should force through necessary economic reforms whether the population liked them or not, she said, while another 40 percent thought reforms should be scrapped if the majority did not support them.

This split clearly runs along party lines, she said, with two-thirds of voters who back Kohl's centre-right coalition arguing for a tough stand on reforms and almost half the supporters of the opposition SPD and Greens against it.

Koecher said 55 percent of those polled opposed a cut in pension benefits that the Kohl government has proposed. Less than 20 percent supported other reform ideas like taxing pensions or having people retire later.
Voters were not impressed with industry's efforts to deal with the current pressure to cut spending either, she said.
A wide majority -- 82 percent of those polled -- felt that large companies did not care about their workers when they slimmed down to improve their competitive position.
Sixty-nine percent felt that relations between management and workers had become worse in recent years.

The idea that capital and labour have common interests -- a foundation stone of the consensus that has characterised Bonn's postwar economy -- has 43 percent support in western Germany and only 22 percent support in the ex-communist east.
